sentences.text: Tehuelchesaurus was a moderately large sauropod dinosaur that lived in Argentina during the Late Jurassic.
Its vertebrae are unique because all dorsal and presacral centra are opisthocoelous, a feature that separates it from Barapasaurus and Patagosaurus.
Measurements of the humerus and femur suggest the animal reached a length of 15 meters, a height of 6 meters, and a weight of 10 tonnes.
Skin impressions show the skin was covered in flat, hexagonal scales arranged in a rosette pattern, which differs from the overlapping scales seen in modern lizards.
The holotype specimen is a 50 percent complete skeleton that includes ten articulated presacral vertebrae, four sacral vertebrae, and various limb bones.
The genus name honors the Tehuelche people, the native inhabitants of the Chubut province where the fossils were found in the Cañadón Calcáreo Formation.
Rich and colleagues named the species Tehuelchesaurus benitezii in 1999 to honor Aldo Benitez, who discovered the holotype.
Indeterminate theropod teeth were found alongside the sauropod remains.
The forelimb anatomy includes a short and robust humerus with strongly expanded ends and a thin middle shaft.
Other skeletal features include anterior dorsal ribs shaped like planks and a puboischiadic contact reaching half the length of the pubis.
A 2019 analysis by Mannion et al. classified Tehuelchesaurus as a basal member of Turiasauria.
Recent phylogenetic analysis places the genus within Camarasauromorpha, related to Camarasaurus and Galveosaurus, but outside Titanosauriformes.
Research indicates that Tehuelchesaurus forms a distinct clade with Galvesaurus, supported by shared traits such as plank-shaped anterior dorsal ribs and a lateral femoral protuberance.
This dinosaur lived approximately 155 to 147 million years ago in what is now South America.
Some researchers consider the presence of sharp posterior pleurocoels on the anterior dorsal vertebrae to be a possible derived trait.
